planting.note: Propagate only from rooted basal offsets that show stable variegation, since seed-grown selloum reverts to solid green; grow in rich, chunky, well-drained mix in bright indirect light to preserve the cream sectoring.

directions: This sport of the common tree philodendron carries irregular cream-to-white sectoring across its deeply lobed, arching leaves, giving the same bold trunk-forming silhouette as green selloum but with striking patchwork variegation on each frond. Because the variegation is unstable, plants sometimes throw solid-green or nearly all-white shoots, which growers typically remove to keep the balance of color and vigor even; more consistently variegated cuttings command a premium among aroid collectors. Give it more light than plain selloum to sustain the pale patches, since white tissue lacks chlorophyll and can scorch in direct sun while too much shade encourages reversion to green. Otherwise it shares selloum's tolerance for large containers or in-ground planting in frost-free climates and its need for ample room to spread as it matures.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from an established clump and pot into chunky, well-drained aroid mix; give bright indirect light for the strongest gold coloration, since low light shifts new leaves toward plain green.

directions: Golden Goddess is a robust, self-heading (non-vining) philodendron hybrid whose glossy, elongated-heart leaves emerge bright chartreuse-gold and mature to a rich yellow-green, giving a consistently sunny presence without any need for a moss pole or trellis. Its clumping rosette habit and tolerance of average indoor conditions make it a popular substitute for the smaller Prince of Orange or Moonlight where a larger-scale accent plant is wanted. Leaf color is brightest in bright, filtered light; deep shade mutes the gold tones toward green, while harsh direct sun can bleach or scorch the thin-textured foliage. Water when the top inch or two of mix dries and increase humidity to prevent brown leaf-tip dieback typical of self-heading philodendrons in dry indoor air.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root single-node stem cuttings in water or moist sphagnum, then pot into loose, well-drained mix; bright indirect light keeps the foliage its signature neon color instead of fading toward plain green.

directions: Lemon Lime is a trailing heartleaf philodendron cultivar prized for its uniformly bright, almost fluorescent chartreuse-yellow leaves, a more intense and even coloration than the softer lime tones of Brasil or Rio, which both carry contrasting green markings rather than solid neon color. The vivid pigment depends on strong indirect light; in low light the vines revert toward duller green, while a few hours of gentle direct morning sun can intensify the yellow without scorching established plants. As a vigorous, fast-trailing vine it works well in hanging baskets, on a shelf where it can cascade, or trained up a small support, and it roots readily from stem cuttings for quick propagation. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and wipe dust from the thin leaves periodically to keep them photosynthesizing efficiently.

planting.note: Divide offsets from a mature clump or root stem cuttings, then grow in chunky, well-drained aroid mix in bright indirect light; this self-heading form needs no climbing support.

directions: Imperial Green is the all-green sibling of the well-known Imperial Red, a compact, self-heading Philodendron erubescens selection with large, glossy, broadly oval leaves held on thick, upright petioles in a tight rosette rather than climbing. Where Imperial Red pushes wine-red new growth, Imperial Green emerges in a paler apple-green that deepens to glossy dark green as leaves mature, giving a cleaner, uniformly green architectural look popular in interior plantscaping and lobby containers. Its sturdy, non-vining habit tolerates handling and lower humidity better than many climbing philodendrons, making it a durable choice for offices and larger interior spaces. Provide bright indirect light and allow the top few inches of mix to dry between thorough waterings to avoid stem rot in the dense crown.

planting.note: Divide basal offsets from an established clump and pot into very well-drained, chunky aroid mix; keep warm and humid, since this Sulawesi species resents cold, soggy conditions.

directions: Native to Sulawesi, this distinctive Alocasia species earns its Rhino Horn nickname from the dramatically elongated, undulating, wavy-margined leaves held on dark, coarsely hairy petioles that curve upward like horns. The narrow, silvery-green leaf blades carry sunken, contrastingly dark veins and a matte, slightly puckered surface quite different from the rounder, glossier leaves of more common alocasias like Polly or Frydek. It is a clumping, moderately compact species well suited to a bright windowsill or grow-light shelf rather than floor space. Provide very free-draining, chunky mix, warm temperatures, and high humidity, and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings to protect the fine feeder roots from rot.

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets and pot into very well-drained, chunky aroid mix; keep warm and consistently humid, since this Philippine species stalls or declines below 60°F.

directions: Endemic to the Philippines, Alocasia clypeolata bears shield-shaped (peltate-leaning), heavily quilted grey-green leaves with a faint metallic sheen and darker sunken veining, a bullate texture that catches light differently than the flat or glossy foliage of most collection alocasias. Its compact clumping habit and modest mature size make it well suited to close-range display on a shelf or terrarium-adjacent setup where the leaf texture can be appreciated. Like most fine-textured alocasias it is sensitive to cold, drafts, and waterlogged mix, so pair very free-draining media with steady warmth and humidity above 50 percent. Reduce watering slightly in winter when growth slows, and repot only when clearly rootbound since disturbed roots are slow to recover in this species.

common_name: Large Anise Tree (Cream-Flowered Collector's Illicium Species)

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in a sheltered, part-to-full-shade site with moist, humus-rich, acidic soil; give it wind protection and mulch the root zone, since this species is still uncommon in Gulf South cultivation and benefits from a gentle establishment period.

directions: A little-grown relative of Florida anise, this species from the mountain forests of southwest China, Myanmar, and Vietnam carries unusually large, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves and clusters of creamy-primrose flowers blushed with pink that open along the branches in spring, releasing a light lemony-elderflower scent rather than the medicinal odor typical of the genus. In cultivation outside its native range it tends to stay shrubby rather than reaching tree size, forming a dense, upright specimen useful as a distinctive woodland-garden accent for collectors. Give it consistent moisture, dappled to full shade, and shelter from drying winds, since it is still considered scarce in specialty nursery trade and performs best when treated as a choice, protected planting rather than a mainstream landscape shrub.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Oliver's Plum Yew (Shade-Tolerant Chinese Conifer Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this species tolerates a wider range of soils than Japanese plum yew but still appreciates shelter from cold, drying winter winds at its northern hardiness limit.

directions: Distinct from the more familiar Cephalotaxus harringtonia, Oliver's plum yew is a dense, broad-spreading evergreen conifer from the subtropical forests of southern China, naturally adapted to growing under a closed forest canopy in deep shade. Its needle-like leaves are held in a looser, more spiraled arrangement than the flat-ranked foliage of Japanese plum yew, giving mature plants a fuller, bushier silhouette that works well as a large-scale shade groundcover or informal hedge beneath high tree canopy. Like other plum yews it is deer-resistant, slow-growing, and untroubled by root competition or heavy shade, making it a durable choice for difficult dry-shade sites once established. It is still uncommon outside conifer specialty collections in the U.S., so plants are best sourced from dedicated conifer nurseries.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun; Kembu is slower-growing and more compact than most heterophyllus cultivars, so it suits tighter foundation or entry plantings.

directions: Kembu ('sword dance' in Japanese) is a slow, upright false holly cultivar whose narrow, gently twisted leaves carry gray-green centers edged in creamy white, giving the plant a softer, more textured variegation than the bolder blocky patterns of Variegatus or Aureomarginatus. New growth emerges with a subtle pink flush before settling into its mature coloring, and small, sweetly fragrant white flowers appear in fall along the stems. It carries noticeably fewer spines than typical heterophyllus selections, making it easier to place and maintain near paths and seating areas. Site it in dappled shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun to keep the variegation crisp rather than bleached.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Golden Osmanthus (Jin Gui Fragrant Tea Olive)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to morning sun; this golden-flowered form is traditionally grown for its heavy, richly scented fall bloom and benefits from a sheltered courtyard-style planting.

directions: Known in China as jin gui, or 'golden osmanthus,' this natural form of sweet olive produces a deeper, richer gold-yellow flower than the pale cream of the typical species and the soft butter tones of cultivars like Fudingzhu, making it one of the most intensely fragrant fall-blooming forms grown for tea and culinary use. The dense, glossy, dark-green foliage holds its color year-round on a large, long-lived evergreen shrub that can be trained as a small specimen tree over time. Its late-summer-into-fall flowering coincides with the Mid-Autumn Festival in its native range, when the fragrance is prized for scenting tea and pastries. Give it well-drained soil and morning sun with afternoon shade protection in the hottest parts of the Gulf South to prevent leaf scorch.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Mayhan Strain Oregon Grape (Dwarf Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Mayhan Strain stays notably lower and denser than the species, so it fits foundation plantings where standard Oregon grape would grow too large.

directions: This selected strain of Oregon grape holly is valued for its naturally dwarf, dense habit and fewer leaflets per leaf than the species, giving the foliage a tidier, more refined look while retaining the glossy, holly-like texture and bronze-to-purple winter color typical of the genus. Bright-yellow spring flower clusters give way to powdery blue-black berries that draw songbirds and can be used for jelly, continuing the ornamental interest into summer. Its compact size makes it far easier to place in foundation and border plantings than the larger straight species, without sacrificing drought tolerance or deer resistance once established. Grow it in dappled shade with good drainage, since standing winter moisture is the most common cause of decline in Oregon grape plantings.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Marvel's rigid, upright stems make it well suited to narrow side yards and tight shaded gaps where a wide-spreading shrub would not fit.

directions: A Southern Living Plant Collection introduction bred as a larger, more vigorous companion to Soft Caress, Marvel carries long, fern-like whorls of dark-green leaflets on stiffly upright, sparsely branched stems, giving it a bold, architectural texture unlike any other mahonia in common cultivation. Fragrant yellow flower spikes open in late fall to early winter and mature into clusters of powdery blue-black berries that persist into the cooler months and attract birds. Its narrow, rigid growth habit holds up well in confined shaded spaces without staking or heavy pruning, and it shares the genus's tolerance for dry shade and deer pressure once roots are established. Site it out of harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the thin leaflets, and provide organically rich, well-drained soil for best performance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant a whole, slightly sprouted fruit on its side at a 45-degree angle with the narrow (stem) end up and just barely covered, once soil is reliably warm; this University of Florida-favored smooth green selection needs the full length of the Gulf Coast growing season to size up before first frost.

directions: Florida Green is the standard smooth, light-green, pear-shaped chayote cultivar recommended by University of Florida IFAS Extension for home gardens across the state, prized for consistent fruit set even through the region's oppressive summer humidity. Fruits run six ounces to a pound and are lightly grooved but essentially spineless, making them easier to handle and peel than heirloom spiny types. Give the sprawling vine a very sturdy arbor or fence, since a single well-sited plant can cover several hundred square feet and yield dozens of fruit from late summer into the first hard freeze. Along the Gulf Coast the rootstock often survives mild winters and resprouts, so mulching the crown heavily after dieback can save a year of establishment.

planting.note: Bury the whole fruit on its side with the pointed stem end tilted upward and just above the soil line after the last frost; this pale-skinned cultivar, named for the North Florida research station where it was selected, benefits from a warm, sheltered planting spot to get the long vine established early.

directions: Monticello White is a cream-to-pale-skinned chayote cultivar, one of the two commercially cloned selections most commonly sold at Florida garden centers alongside Florida Green, and named for the north Florida city near the research station associated with its selection. Its smooth, ivory fruit is slightly milder and more tender-skinned than the common green types, and it is prized in home gardens both for fresh eating and for its ornamental pale coloring on the vine. Like all chayote it needs a season of six months or more of warmth to fruit heavily, so Gulf Coast growers should plant as early as safely possible after frost and provide a large, strong trellis. The vine's large starchy tuberous root, which develops after a full growing season, is also edible and can be dug and cooked like a yam once the vine dies back for winter.

planting.note: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep after soil has warmed well past last frost and inoculate seed with a cowpea-type Rhizobium; Endurance's weakly perennial habit means an established stand in mild Gulf Coast winters can resprout from the crown the following spring instead of needing full replanting.

directions: Endurance was bred by crossing the widely grown forage cultivar Rongai with a vigorous wild perennial accession from Zimbabwe (CPI 24973), then released as a weakly perennial lablab selection for tropical and subtropical forage systems. Unlike standard annual lablab cultivars, established Endurance stands can regrow from the crown into a second and even third growing season after grazing, mowing, or cutting, provided winters stay mild, making it a candidate for reduced-replanting cover cropping in zone 9 and warmer. It climbs and sprawls vigorously, fixes nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis, and produces heavy biomass valued for grazing, green manure, or trellised summer cover in the Gulf South. Because true commercial seed supply is limited compared to Rongai or Highworth, gardeners wanting Endurance may need to source it through tropical forage seed banks or university research collections.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after soil is thoroughly warm; Smooth Boy is a reliable smooth-skinned selection recommended by University of Florida extension programs, harvested young for cooking or left to mature and dry for sponges.

directions: Smooth Boy is a widely available named cultivar of smooth luffa, recommended by University of Florida gardening programs for home dual-purpose growing: young fruit picked at 6-8 inches has mild, zucchini-like flesh good for stir-fries and soups, while fruit left on the vine to mature and turn brown yields the classic fibrous bath and cleaning sponge once peeled and cured. It produces cylindrical, smooth to faintly ribbed fruit on a fast-climbing vine that thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity, and it flowers with showy bright-yellow blossoms that attract pollinators. Give it a tall, strong trellis or arbor, since vines readily reach 15-20 feet, and keep soil evenly moist through fruit set for the straightest, best-formed sponges.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Lucky Boy is a named angled-luffa selection recommended by Florida extension resources for its productive, mild-flavored young fruit.

directions: Lucky Boy is a named cultivar of ridged (angled) luffa grown for its deeply ten-ribbed, dark-green fruit, harvested young at 6-8 inches when the flesh is still tender, mild, and free of the fibrous skeleton that develops later. It is favored in South and Southeast Asian home gardens and by Florida growers for heavier, more reliable fruit set through hot, humid summers than smooth luffa types, and it climbs vigorously on a trellis, fence, or arbor. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine productive continuously from early summer through fall in Gulf Coast conditions. Young shoots and leaves are also edible and used in some Southeast Asian cooking, though the fruit is the primary crop.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing and plant after soil is thoroughly warm; this narrow, spiny-warted Indian-type bitter melon needs a long hot stretch and a sturdy trellis to produce well.

directions: Indian Long is the slender, pointed-ended bitter melon type covered in sharp, jagged, triangular ridges rather than the smooth warts typical of Chinese and Taiwanese cultivars, and it carries the sharper, more assertive bitterness favored in Indian and Vietnamese cooking. Fruits are best picked young and firm, 6-9 inches long, while still glossy green, for use in stuffed karela, stir-fries, and curries; the intense bitterness mellows somewhat with salting, parboiling, or frying. The vigorous climbing vine performs well in Gulf Coast heat and humidity but benefits from a strong trellis and consistent moisture during fruit set to avoid stress-induced flower drop. Seeds have a hard, slow-to-imbibe coat, so nicking or an overnight soak speeds germination noticeably.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; this Caucasus native spreads gradually by rhizomes and resents disturbance once established.

directions: Native to the Colchis region of the western Caucasus and northeastern Turkey, this butcher's broom is distinguished from the far more common Ruscus aculeatus by its notably larger, tongue-shaped cladodes up to seven inches long that are completely spineless and softer in texture, held on slow-spreading, clump-forming stems. Tiny flowers are borne directly on the flattened cladode surface and, on female plants growing near a male, give way to glossy scarlet berries that persist through winter. It tolerates deep dry shade and heavy root competition beneath mature trees better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen, needing only an annual thinning of old canes at the base to keep the clump tidy. Because it spreads slowly and stays under two feet, it works well as a refined woodland-floor accent rather than the coarser groundcover role often given to the spinier species.

common_name: Christmas Berry Butcher's Broom (Dwarf Self-Fruiting Ruscus)

planting.note: Plant in spring in any well-drained soil in dry shade; this Irish-bred dwarf selection needs no companion plant to fruit and stays compact enough for a small bed or container.

directions: Selected in Ireland in the early 2000s, 'Christmas Berry' is a slow-growing dwarf form of butcher's broom with spiny cladodes packed densely along short, congested stems, forming a tight patch roughly a foot across even after several years. Unlike most butcher's broom cultivars, which need separate male and female plants to set fruit, this selection carries functionally bisexual flowers and reliably covers itself in glossy red berries every winter without a pollinator partner. It shrugs off deep shade, drought, and poor soil once established, making it a practical low-mounding accent for a shaded rock garden or the front of a dry woodland border where its diminutive scale would be lost among larger shrubs. Wear gloves when handling or dividing it, as the cladode tips are sharply spine-pointed.

common_name: Ghorepani Sweet Box (Compact Narrow-Leaf Himalayan Sarcococca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; 'Ghorepani' is a compact, upright selection of the true Himalayan species collected near the Nepali village of the same name.

directions: Collected near Ghorepani in the Nepal Himalaya and later given a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, this selection of the true species (var. hookeriana, as opposed to the more commonly sold dwarf var. humilis or narrow var. digyna) forms a neat, upright, suckering clump of glossy, sword-shaped leaves on slender maroon-tinted stems. Clusters of tiny, thread-like white flowers open in the depths of winter and release a powerful sweet fragrance out of proportion to their size, followed by shining black fruit. Its habit is noticeably more upright and self-contained than the spreading var. humilis, making it a good choice where a defined clump rather than a loose colony is wanted near a shaded entry or path. Grow in reliably moist, humus-rich soil and mulch annually; established plants tolerate dry shade and root competition from nearby trees.

common_name: Pepperspot Aucuba (Compact Male Fine-Speckled Japanese Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in ordinary, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; as a male clone 'Pepperspot' produces no berries but is a reliable pollen source for female aucubas planted nearby.

directions: 'Pepperspot' is a British-raised male cultivar of Japanese laurel with glossy, waxy, toothed leaves finely dusted in small, uniform yellow flecks, giving a much subtler, more evenly peppered look than the bold blotching of older gold-dust selections. Small maroon flowers with bright yellow stamens appear in spring but, being a male clone, are followed by no fruit. It forms a dense, rounded bush that tolerates deep dry shade, root competition, and neglect better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen, and can be sheared into a substantial informal hedge or screen. Grow in any well-drained soil and water only during extended drought once established; its main garden role is as a tough, low-maintenance backdrop and a dependable pollinator for berrying female aucubas.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in ordinary, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; 'Marmorata' is a female cultivar that needs a male aucuba such as 'Golden King' or the species type nearby to set its showy red berries.

directions: Long grown in English collections before being reintroduced to American nurseries from Hillier's arboretum stock, 'Marmorata' carries thick, leathery leaves marked with a heavier, more irregularly marbled gold pattern than the fine speckling of 'Crotonifolia' or 'Picturata', giving a coarser, more painterly variegation from a distance. Inconspicuous small purple flowers in spring are followed, on plants grown with a male pollinator, by generous clusters of large red berries that persist through winter and brighten the evergreen shrub in the darkest months. It is exceptionally tolerant of dry shade, salt exposure, and urban pollution, thriving under dense tree canopy or in narrow foundation beds where few other broadleaf evergreens perform. Full sun deepens the gold marbling but risks leaf scorch, so light to full shade with occasional moisture during drought gives the best appearance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Whitewater was bred for improved resistance to the leaf-spot fungi that commonly disfigure older leucothoe cultivars.

directions: Patented as 'HOWW' and sold under the trademark Whitewater, this selection emerges each spring in soft pink, copper, and green tones before settling into narrow, arching leaves edged with a fine, consistent ivory margin, a subtler and more refined variegation pattern than the bold pink-and-cream mottling of 'Rainbow' or 'Girard's Rainbow'. Small white, urn-shaped flowers hang from red stems in spring, and the foliage turns shades of crimson and scarlet in autumn and winter. Its most valuable trait is improved resistance to the leaf-spot and dieback fungi that often disfigure older drooping leucothoe cultivars in humid climates, and it is rated hardy to a notably colder zone 5b. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in filtered light to full shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun that can scorch the variegated margins.

common_name: Burning Love Leucothoe (Mid-Size Red-New-Growth Keiske's Doghobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; this Dutch-bred selection of Leucothoe keiskei grows noticeably larger and more upright than the dwarf 'Royal Ruby' clone.

directions: Bred in the Netherlands and marketed under the Leafscape banner alongside the fontanesiana selection 'Little Flames', Burning Love is a compact, multi-stemmed selection of the dwarf Japanese species Leucothoe keiskei that grows a foot or more taller and wider than the low-mounding 'Royal Ruby' clone, giving it a more upright, shrubby presence. New shoots emerge a vivid fiery red before maturing to glossy dark green, and cold weather brings on deep burgundy winter tones across the whole plant rather than just the newest growth. Terminal clusters of drooping, cylindrical white flowers appear from late spring into early summer, larger individually than those of the more common fontanesiana and axillaris types. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from hot afternoon sun, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.
